title: VB9-05507
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated June 24, 2019, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellants), are citizens of India from a village in Rajasthan. They appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated June 24, 2019, rejecting their claims for refugee protection. The RPD found that the cities of Ludhiana, Amritsar and Mumbai present as viable Internal Flight Alternatives (IFA).
The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in its decision, and request that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD for re-determination.
I do not find that the RPD has erred in its decision. For the reasons that follow, the decision of the RPD is confirmed.

The Appellants are a young married couple of the Sikh faith. The Principal Appellant owns approximately XXXX acres of land outside of the village of XXXX XXXX, Rajasthan and was an XXXX XXXX. The Associate Appellant was a XXXX.1The Principal Appellant alleges that he had problems with the police in his village of XXXX XXXX, Rajasthan, after hiring a worker/labourer from Uttar Pardesh in XXXX 2017. 2

The worker was taken into police custody in XXXX 2017, for not having proper documentation and the Principal Appellant was threatened and detained for XXXX days for refusing to pay a large bribe to the police.

In XXXX 2017, the village police returned to the Appellants' property and located a gun in the worker's room, which they had searched without the worker or Principal Appellant being present. The Principal Appellant was detained again by the XXXX XXXX police for refusing to sign a document confirming that the worker's room had been searched in his presence. He was held for XXXX days and beaten while detained.
The Associate Appellant provided a complaint letter to the XXXX XXXX of Police, to a court officer, and to the XXXX XXXX in Jaipur, and was taken in for police questioning on XXXX XXXX, 2017.
The Appellants went into hiding in New Delhi. They obtained visas for Canada in XXXX 2018, but were not able to leave India until XXXX XXXX, 2018, because they did not have enough money.
They made their claims for refugee protection shortly after their arrival in Canada.

The jurisprudence establishes that the RAD is required to undertake an independent assessment of the evidence and reach its own determination. Deference is owed to the RPD only where the RPD held a meaningful advantage in assessing evidence.3
In the present case, I see no reason to show deference to any of the RPD's findings, and as a result I have applied a correctness standard.

In coming to a decision, I have independently assessed the evidence and arguments and with respect to the claim of the Associate Appellant, I have considered the Guideline on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender Related Persecution.4

The Appellants argue that the RPD decision is based on speculation and that no weight was given to the evidence presented. I do not agree. I find that the RPD considered and weighed the evidence in the RPD record in coming to its decision. The RPD also considered 38 pages of post-hearing evidence which it received on June 14, 2019.5
In my independent assessment of the evidence, I find that the RPD has not speculated in determining that the Appellants enjoy multiple IFAs in India. IFA
Although not explicit under section 96 of the IRPA6, an IFA is an integral part of the Convention refugee definition.
Once an IFA has been proposed, the onus shifts to the Appellants to show that they do not have an IFA.

The test to be applied in determining whether there is an IFA is two-pronged.7 a) The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of persecution in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and no risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or torture. b) The conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the Appellants, for them to seek refuge there.
The RPD correctly identified IFA as an issue at the beginning of the hearing and the Appellants were given notice that the cities of Ludhiana, Amritsar and Mumbai were potential IFA locations.

The RPD heard the testimony of the Appellants on this issue. The Appellants were represented by an unpaid representative before the RPD. That same counsel represents them on appeal. Their counsel was able to ask questions and provided submissions.

In my independent assessment of the evidence, I find that the Appellants have not established that they would face persecution or a risk to their lives in the proposed IFA locations. IFA first prong - no serious possibility of persecution and no risk to life

I find that the RPD did not speculate in finding that the Appellants could relocate to the identified IFA locations. In its decision the RPD acknowledged that the Appellants provided evidence that they had been targeted and harmed by the police in the village of XXXX XXXX on numerous occasions. The RPD also determined that based on the evidence presented, the risk they face extended to the entire district of XXXX XXXX, which is responsible for the police in their home village of XXXX XXXX. The problems that the Appellants have alleged in their village are not in dispute.

I find that the Appellants have not established that the local police from their village or the larger district would have an interest in pursuing them to one of the IFA locations. The problems faced by the Appellants are at a village or local level. While there may be some evidence that the local police have enquired with the Principal Appellant's father as to the Appellants' whereabouts, there is no evidence that charges were ever laid against the Principal Appellant or his wife or that they would be pursued to one of the IFA locations outside of Rajasthan.

The Appellants argue that they are at risk of being found and harmed throughout the country. I do not find that this has been established in the independent review of the documents and testimony before me.

In its decision the RPD acknowledges the evidence before that division including documents provided by the Appellants and documents in the National Documentation Package (NDP) indicating that corruption and police misconduct are widespread in India, and pointing out that media articles presented by the Appellants describe a lack of accountability for police deaths in custody.8

However, there is also objective evidence from the NDP referenced in the RPD decision which describes a lack of connectivity between police stations in the country. A Response to Information Request (RIR) in the NDP describes how, "there is little inter-state police communication except for cases of major crimes like smuggling, terrorism, and some high-profile organised crime".9

One source in this Response to Information Request, states that police stations across India are "virtually unconnected islands in the case of crime and criminal tracking. There is no system of effective data storage.....sharing and accessing data," and there is "no single system" by which a police unit can "talk to another directly".10
The objective evidence indicates that there have been difficulties linking police stations into a single network, and that stations work in silos as far as criminal information is concerned.11

The Appellants argue that they are at risk of persecution by agents of the state and therefore there is no IFA. They also point out in their memorandum that a person of interest can easily be located by the police through registration as a tenant, and that no one can hide in India without the knowledge of the police.

With respect to tenant registration, this system may exist to some degree in India, but it is not effective. The Appellants provided several media articles relating to tenant verification, including reports of convictions.12 Objective evidence in the NDP indicates that "police verification, in theory, is meant to ensure that if a criminal or terrorist is seeking tenancy, the police know and keep an eye. It also ensures the safety of the property owner, who can escape allegations or complicity in a crime, in case a crime is committed, by saying that he had informed the police".13

This same report also indicates that "it is impossible for the police to actually verify the identity of all those who rent property", and that "the police force is not equipped to personally go and check all new tenants".14

A home office report in the NDP indicates that, "India does not have a centralised registration system in place to enable police to check the whereabouts of inhabitants in their own state, let alone in other states or union territories".15
I find that given the low profile of the Appellants, they would not face a serious possibility of persecution or a risk to their lives on a balance of probabilities in the IFA locations.

In my independent assessment of the evidence I find that there is insufficient credible evidence establishing that the agents of harm would be able or even motivated to locate the Appellants if they relocate to one of the proposed IFA locations. I agree with the RPDs finding, that despite any localized risks that the Appellants may face, there is insufficient evidence to find that they face a risk across all of India, particularly outside of the state of Rajasthan, which is where all three of the proposed IFA locations are situated. Associate Appellant

The Associate Appellant testified that she is at risk of experiencing sexual violence in India. The objective evidence in the NDP describes incidents of violence against women including rape, kidnapping and abduction. The objective documents also indicate that violence against women is often under-reported.16 In the post hearing evidence provided by the Appellants, documents include reports in the media about India being the most dangerous country in the world to be a woman because of the high risk of sexual violence and slave labour.17

While the objective evidence indicates that crimes against women including sexual violence occurs in India, I find that the objective evidence alone does not establish that the Associate Appellant will face a serious possibility of persecution if she is to return to the country and relocates to one of the proposed IFA locations. Not all of the women in Ludhiana, Amritsar and Mumbai face gender-based violence. While single women and widows may be considered as "more vulnerable" than others18, the Associate Appellant is married and will be with her husband, mitigating any risk she may face. I find that overall, the Associate Appellant has failed to establish with sufficient trustworthy and credible evidence that she will face a serious possibly of sexual or gender-based violence in Ludhiana, Amritsar or Mumbai. IFA second prong - reasonableness of relocation to proposed IFAs

I have made my own independent assessment of the evidence in light of the personal circumstances of the Appellants and the circumstances in the proposed IFA. I find that it is not objectively unreasonable for the Appellants to relocate to one of the proposed IFA locations.

The court has set a very high threshold for what makes an IFA unreasonable in all of the circumstances. The standard is high and requires proof of adverse conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of the Appellants in travelling to and living in the IFA locations.19

The Appellants are young, mobile and resourceful. The Principal Appellant has completed secondary school education and XXXX years of college or university level education. The Associate Appellant has completed a university degree.

While they have not demonstrated a work history beyond XXXX and house work, they do indicate a desire for employment positions in XXXX and XXXX.20 There is no evidence before me to show that motivated individuals, such as the Appellants, would not be able to find employment and be able to support themselves in one of the identified IFA locations.

The Appellants speak Punjabi and English 21 which are languages spoken across the country. According to a report from Australia, an estimated 125 million people speak English as either a first, second or third language.22 The objective evidence describes India as a diverse, multi-ethnic, multi-lingual society with a law providing for freedom of movement granting citizen the right to reside and settle in any part of the country.23 Punjabi is the primary language in the state of Punjab,24 which is where Ludhiana and Amritsar are located.

Objective evidence in the NDP indicates that, India is the 8th largest country in the world by area, and has an estimated population of nearly 1,282 billion. There are more than 50 urban areas in India which have a population of over 1 million.25 India is described as a stable democracy with regular and largely peaceful elections at the national and state levels.26

The cities of Amritsar and Ludhiana are both located in the state of Punjab where Sikhs are a majority. Both are cities with over a million people. The Sikh population of India is approximately 19 million. Ludhiana is the largest city in Punjab in terms of area and population and is also the industrial hub of the Punjab state. Ludhiana has an estimated population of over 1.6 million people.27
Mumbai is India's largest city, located in the state of Maharashtra, with a population over 18 million. It is the financial centre of the country. 28

Having considered all of the evidence, I find that that Appellants have not established on a balance of probabilities that it would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh to move to the cities of Ludhiana, Amritsar or Mumbai.

I have reviewed the Appellants testimony, documentary evidence, arguments, and have undertaken my own analysis to find that the RPD did not err when it found that the Appellants have viable IFAs in Ludhiana, Amritsar or Mumbai.
Since having a viable IFA is fatal to claims made under both sections 96 and 97(1)29 of the IRPA, I find that the Appellants' claims fail on both grounds.

For all these reasons, I find that there is no serious possibility of persecution for the Appellants in Ludhiana, Amritsar or Mumbai, and no risk to life, or risk of cruel and unusual treatment of punishment or danger of torture.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
